claims.text: The starting material consists of crystalline nanoparticles.
The starting nanoparticles are near-equiatomic solid solutions containing at least five metals.
The proposed intervention is to add minor amounts of refractory elements such as Mo and W.
Minor Mo and W additions can produce solid-solution strengthening.
Adding Mo and W increases the atomic-size difference among the alloying elements.
The increased atomic-size difference produces a stronger solid-solution-strengthening effect.
Solid-solution strengthening caused by refractory additions enhances nanoparticle stability during operation at 773–1173 K.
Refractory-modified nanoparticles will be more stable than untreated nanoparticles in the 773–1173 K catalytic regime.
Refractory-modified nanoparticles may have improved catalytic performance relative to untreated nanoparticles.
Minor refractory additions can remain compatible with a multielement solid-solution alloy.
The intervention is expected to be effective broadly for near-equiatomic nanoparticles containing five or more metals.
The optimal amount of refractory addition is unknown.
Interactions between the refractory additions and the other alloying elements are uncertain.

contradictions.description: Catalytic improvement is presented only as a potential secondary outcome, but the falsification rule treats lack of enhanced catalytic performance as part of the failure condition. This makes it unclear whether stability alone is the decisive endpoint.
